title: Does every isotropic log-concave measure have a dimension-free Poincaré constant?
formal: Does there exist a universal constant C<∞ such that, for every dimension n≥1, every isotropic log-concave probability measure μ on ℝⁿ, and every locally Lipschitz f:ℝⁿ→ℝ with finite second moment and finite gradient energy, $\operatorname{Var}_\mu(f)\le C\int\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\,d\mu(x)$? This is the Poincaré formulation of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
definitions: The measure has a Lebesgue density ρ=e^{−V}, where V:ℝⁿ→ℝ∪{+∞} is convex and ∫ρ=1; allowing V=+∞ includes uniform distributions on full-dimensional convex bodies. Isotropy means ∫x dμ(x)=0 and ∫xxᵀ dμ(x)=Iₙ. Variance is Varμ(f)=∫(f−∫f dμ)²dμ, and ∇f is the almost-everywhere Euclidean gradient. Let C_P(μ) be the infimum of constants that make the displayed inequality hold for all the stated f. The requested bound is supₙ supμ C_P(μ)<∞, with μ ranging over isotropic log-concave measures in ℝⁿ. There is no symmetry, product structure, smoothness, or positive lower curvature bound on V. The universal constant may depend on none of n, μ, or f. In the isoperimetric convention used by the recent papers, ψμ is the reciprocal Cheeger expansion constant; ψμ² is comparable to C_P(μ) up to universal factors. Thus a bound on ψμ must be squared when expressed as a bound on the Poincaré constant used here.
answer_criterion: Answer yes by proving one finite constant valid for all dimensions, measures, and test functions. Answer no by constructing isotropic log-concave measures and test functions whose variance-to-gradient-energy ratios are unbounded. Proving the inequality only for linear or quadratic functions, or with a factor growing with n, does not resolve this statement.
context:
The inequality asks whether a function can vary substantially across a log-concave distribution while changing only slowly in the regions where that distribution places mass. Isotropy fixes the scale: each unit-direction linear function already has variance one and gradient energy one. The conjecture says that nonlinear functions cannot create an arbitrarily larger ratio as dimension grows.

The geometric version rules out a hidden bottleneck separating two substantial portions of the measure. For a log-concave density, the conjecture says that the best arbitrary separating set has boundary expansion comparable to an appropriate halfspace cut. Uniform distributions on convex bodies are included, so the question is not confined to smooth, strongly convex potentials where curvature can directly control a spectral gap.

The original algorithmic motivation was sampling by random walks. Poor expansion can trap a local walk in one part of a body for a long time; good expansion bounds its mixing. Sampling then supports volume estimation, integration, and convex optimization. A KLS theorem would improve the geometric ingredient in these analyses, though total algorithmic complexity would still account for access to the body, initialization, and the chosen walk.

Thin-shell concentration concerns the special observable ‖X‖₂. Klartag and Lehec’s 2025 result, revised in February 2026, bounds E(‖X‖₂−√n)² by a universal constant. This settles thin-shell concentration and also supports the resolved slicing question, but does not by itself control every test function in the Poincaré inequality. These neighboring geometric conjectures must therefore be tracked separately.

The remaining dimension dependence is small but substantive. Klartag’s 2023 theorem gives C_P(μ)=O(log n). Letwin’s July 2026 preprint reports a dimension-free inequality for quadratic forms and derives ψμ=O((log n)^{1/4}), hence C_P(μ)=O(√log n). The latter is a reported preprint improvement, and even that estimate still leaves a growing factor rather than the universal constant required here.
why: KLS links the geometry of high-dimensional convex sets to spectral gaps, concentration, and the efficiency of sampling. It asks whether covariance normalization alone removes every dimension-dependent bottleneck for log-concave measures, making it a central structural question behind continuous randomized algorithms.

importance.reason: A foundational high-dimensional geometry conjecture with substantial consequences for sampling, integration, optimization, and concentration inequalities.

progress.text: Kannan, Lovász, and Simonovits formulate the isoperimetric conjecture in connection with localization and random-walk sampling in convex bodies.
Klartag and Lehec obtain the first polylogarithmic bounds for the KLS isoperimetric constant using stochastic-localization techniques.
Klartag proves ψμ=O(√log n), equivalently C_P(μ)=O(log n), through an improved log-concave Lichnerowicz inequality.
Klartag and Lehec settle the thin-shell conjecture. The 23 February 2026 revision controls E(‖X‖₂−√n)² uniformly, a particular radial concentration target rather than the full Poincaré inequality.

Letwin’s preprint reports Var(XᵀMX)≤2E‖∇(XᵀMX)‖₂² for every symmetric M and isotropic log-concave X, and derives ψₙ=O((log n)^{1/4}). In this card’s normalization the resulting general-function bound is C_P=O(√log n), not O((log n)^{1/4}).

status_note: The full KLS conjecture is explicitly open in the primary sources, including Letwin’s July 2026 preprint. Research through 10 September 2026 found no dimension-free general-function resolution. The recent quadratic-form and thin-shell results are not treated as proofs of the full conjecture; the July bound is labeled as a preprint result.
